texts.0: SP, due to an abrupt nose-low input at breakout initiation and an abandoned instrument cross-check, did not maintain the assigned altitude while establishing separation of the flight path. The altitude deviation exceeded 300 feet and continued to diverge without any correction being started. The IP intervened on the controls to arrest the excursion and return the aircraft to level flight.
texts.1: SP, due to a late return to the altimeter after clearing the flight path, did not arrest the altitude excursion generated by the breakout turn. The deviation reached the 300 feet limit and was recovered only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The correction was applied well after the point at which the deviation was already displayed.
texts.2: SP, due to heavy back pressure carried through the initial breakout turn, allowed the altitude to drift from the assigned value while separating from the formation. The excursion reached approximately 200 feet, between the 150 and 300 feet limits. SP identified the trend on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude with no IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude throughout the breakout, keeping deviations within 150 feet while establishing separation of the flight path. Pitch was compensated as bank was applied and the altimeter was cross-checked during the turn away, not only after roll-out.
texts.4: SP flew the breakout with the assigned altitude essentially fixed, the altimeter needle showing only barely readable movement through the turn away. Pitch and bank were coordinated so precisely that no corrective input was required at any stage of the separation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude inside standards during the breakout, but the deviations sat consistently in the upper part of the acceptable band and always in the same direction, a slow climb as bank increased. The altimeter is being consulted after roll-out rather than during the turn away. SP is expected to move the pitch compensation into the initial part of the maneuver so that the excursion never develops.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a late return to the altimeter after clearing the flight path, held the altitude excursion at the 300 foot limit before it was arrested. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the pitch compensation into the initial part of the maneuver so the excursion never develops.
texts_at.2: SP, due to heavy back pressure carried through the initial breakout turn, let the altitude drift to about 200 feet from the assigned value before identifying the trend and returning to it without any IP input. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move the pitch compensation into the initial part of the maneuver so the excursion never develops.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in cross-checking the altimeter during the turn away, maintained the assigned altitude throughout the breakout, keeping deviations to about 100 feet while establishing separation of the flight path. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to move the pitch compensation into the initial part of the maneuver so the excursion never develops.

texts_above.2: SP let the altitude drift to about 200 feet from the assigned value before identifying the trend on the altimeter and returning to it, without any IP input. Cross-checking the altimeter during the turn away, rather than after roll-out, would hold that drift tighter. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control technique during the breakout.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude throughout the breakout, keeping deviations to about 100 feet while establishing separation, cross-checking the altimeter during the turn away and not only after roll-out. The cross-check is already carried through the turn; only the smallest further margin is left to gain. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control technique during the breakout.
texts_above.4: SP flew the breakout with the assigned altitude essentially fixed, deviations inside about 50 feet with pitch and bank coordinated so precisely that no corrective input was required at any stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control technique during the breakout.

texts.0: SP, due to an uncoordinated power reduction applied together with the breakout turn, did not maintain the assigned airspeed while separating from the formation. The airspeed deviation passed 20 knots and kept increasing, degrading the predictability of the separation for the formation leader. The IP took the throttle to restore the assigned airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged as bank and back pressure were applied, did not hold the assigned airspeed through the breakout. The deviation reached the 20 knots limit and was corrected only after the IP called the airspeed twice. The throttle correction was delayed and then over-applied, producing a second excursion in the opposite direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a small lag between the control input and the corresponding power adjustment, allowed the airspeed to drift during the turn away from the formation. The deviation reached about 15 knots, between the 10 and 20 knots limits, and SP recognized it on the airspeed indicator and returned to the assigned value promptly and without IP input.
texts.3: SP held the assigned airspeed throughout the breakout, keeping deviations within 10 knots while establishing separation. Power was adjusted together with the control inputs, so airspeed remained predictable for the formation leader from the initiation of the maneuver.
texts.4: SP flew the breakout with the airspeed practically locked on the assigned value, showing only momentary and negligible movement of the indicator during the turn away. Power and pitch were coordinated so that no airspeed correction was needed at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the airspeed within standards during the breakout, but the values were repeatedly close to the outer part of the acceptable band, always on the fast side after the initial bank input. The power correction is being made in response to the indication rather than anticipated with the control input. SP is expected to lead the power change with the maneuver so the airspeed stays centred on the assigned value.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged as bank and back pressure were applied, reached the 20 knot limit of airspeed deviation before the throttle correction was made. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lead the power change with the maneuver so the airspeed stays centred on the assigned value.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a small lag between the control input and the corresponding power adjustment, let the airspeed drift about 15 knots during the turn away before recognizing it and returning to the assigned value promptly. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the power change with the maneuver so the airspeed stays centred on the assigned value.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in adjusting power together with the control inputs, held the assigned airspeed throughout the breakout, keeping deviations to about 7 knots while establishing separation. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lead the power change with the maneuver so the airspeed stays centred on the assigned value.

texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed drift about 15 knots during the turn away before recognizing it on the indicator and returning to the assigned value promptly, without IP input. Adjusting power together with the control input, rather than a step behind it, would hold that drift tighter. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-lead technique during the breakout.
texts_above.3: SP held the assigned airspeed throughout the breakout, keeping deviations to about 7 knots, with power adjusted together with the control inputs from the initiation of the maneuver. The power lead is already close to the maneuver; only the smallest lag remains to be closed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-lead technique during the breakout.
texts_above.4: SP flew the breakout with the airspeed practically locked on the assigned value, deviations inside about 3 knots with power and pitch coordinated so no correction was needed at any point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-lead technique during the breakout.

texts.0: SP, due to a roll-out started without reference to the intended exit heading, did not establish the aircraft on the heading required to guarantee separation from the formation. The heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the aircraft continued to turn through it, so the geometry of the separation was no longer the one expected by the formation leader. The IP intervened to roll out and establish the correct exit heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan concentrated outside the cockpit after the initial turn away, did not roll out on the required exit heading during the breakout. The heading error reached the 10 degrees limit and was corrected only after the IP stated the required heading. The correction was made late, after the aircraft had already tracked away from the intended separation line.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly high roll rate at the end of the turn away, overshot the required exit heading during the breakout. The error reached approximately 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degrees limits, and SP identified it on the heading indicator and returned to the required heading in a timely manner with no IP input.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the required exit heading at the end of the breakout, holding the heading within 5 degrees while maintaining the separation established. Roll-out was anticipated so that the aircraft settled directly on the intended track away from the formation.
texts.4: SP established the exit heading with the aircraft settling on the required value with no perceptible overshoot or subsequent correction. The heading was then held rock steady while separation was maintained, and the track away from the formation was exactly as required.
texts.marginal: SP held the exit heading within standards, but the roll-out was consistently a few degrees past the required value and then reversed, always in the same direction. The anticipation of the roll-out point is being computed after the heading indicator moves rather than before. SP is expected to lead the roll-out so that the exit heading is captured without a reversal.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a scan concentrated outside the cockpit after the initial turn away, rolled out with the heading error at the 10 degree limit before the correction was made. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the roll-out so the exit heading is captured without a reversal.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a slightly high roll rate at the end of the turn away, overshot the required exit heading by about 8 degrees before identifying it on the heading indicator and returning to the required heading in a timely manner. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lead the roll-out so the exit heading is captured without a reversal.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in anticipating the roll-out point, rolled out on the required exit heading at the end of the breakout, holding the heading within about 3 degrees while maintaining separation. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to lead the roll-out so the exit heading is captured without a reversal.

texts_above.2: SP overshot the required exit heading by about 8 degrees before identifying it on the heading indicator and returning to the required heading in a timely manner, with no IP input. Anticipating the roll-out point before the heading indicator moves would remove that overshoot. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid roll-out anticipation on exit heading.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the required exit heading at the end of the breakout, holding the heading within about 3 degrees, with the roll-out anticipated so the aircraft settled directly on the intended track. The anticipation of the roll-out point already works; only the smallest overshoot remains to be removed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed roll-out anticipation on exit heading.
texts_above.4: SP established the exit heading with the aircraft settling on the required value with no perceptible overshoot, holding it rock steady with a deviation of a degree or two. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding roll-out anticipation on exit heading.

error_modes.label: Recognition of breakout conditions and timeliness of initiation

texts.0: SP, due to continuation of the formation position after the conditions requiring a breakout had clearly been met, did not execute the breakout when it was imposed. The situation was allowed to develop with no separating action initiated at all, and the IP intervened and flew the breakout to restore separation. The maneuver was not executed timely or flawlessly as required, and the necessity for IP intervention was the defining feature of the attempt.
texts.1: SP, due to a decision to hold the position and wait for the situation to resolve itself, did not initiate the breakout at the point at which it was imposed. The maneuver was started only after a direct verbal instruction from the IP, by which time the developing situation had progressed to the limit of what remained acceptable. The initiation was not timely and the requirement to execute without the necessity for IP prompting was not met.
texts.2: SP, due to a short hesitation while reassessing whether the situation genuinely required separation, initiated the breakout later than the point at which the conditions were met. SP then recognized the delay unprompted, committed to the maneuver and completed it correctly without any IP intervention. The execution itself was correct, but the decision time consumed part of the available margin.
texts.3: SP recognized the conditions requiring the breakout as they occurred and initiated the maneuver immediately, without hesitation and without any IP prompting. The breakout was executed timely and flawlessly whenever it was imposed, exactly as required of the wingman.
texts.4: SP identified the developing condition at its earliest indication and initiated the breakout instantly, with the decision made before the situation had any opportunity to develop further. The execution was precise, and the timing demonstrated judgment ahead of the requirement rather than in reaction to it.
texts.marginal: SP initiated every breakout within acceptable time, but the decision was consistently made at the later end of the available window, with a visible pause before committing. The tendency is to verify the condition twice before acting. SP is expected to act on the first clear indication that the conditions are met, since the value of the maneuver lies in its immediacy.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a decision to hold the position and wait for the situation to resolve itself, initiated the breakout at the edge of what remained acceptable, after the developing situation had progressed toward the limit. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to act on the first clear indication that the conditions are met, since the value of the maneuver lies in its immediacy.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a short hesitation while reassessing whether the situation genuinely required separation, initiated the breakout later than the point at which the conditions were met, then recognized the delay unprompted and completed the maneuver correctly. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to act on the first clear indication that the conditions are met, since the value of the maneuver lies in its immediacy.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief pause before committing to the maneuver, recognized the conditions requiring the breakout as they occurred and initiated the maneuver without hesitation and without any IP prompting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to act on the first clear indication that the conditions are met, since the value of the maneuver lies in its immediacy.

texts_above.2: SP initiated the breakout a little later than the point at which the conditions were met, then recognized the delay unprompted, committed to the maneuver and completed it correctly without any IP intervention. Acting on the first clear indication, rather than reassessing it, would remove that hesitation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady breakout initiation timing.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the conditions requiring the breakout as they occurred and initiated the maneuver immediately, without hesitation and without any IP prompting. The recognition is already immediate; only the smallest pause before committing remains to close. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate breakout initiation timing.
texts_above.4: SP identified the developing condition at its earliest indication and initiated the breakout instantly, with the decision made before the situation had any opportunity to develop further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary breakout initiation timing.

error_modes.label: Control inputs establishing positive flight path separation

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs that were both late and of insufficient magnitude, did not apply the timely proper inputs required to ensure break out and separation of the aircraft flight path. The flight paths were not made to diverge and the geometry remained convergent with the formation. The IP intervened on the controls to generate the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a tentative and progressively applied bank input, did not achieve a positive divergence of the flight path at the moment the breakout was required. The inputs were increased to an effective value only after the IP verbally directed a larger displacement, and the separation was therefore achieved late. The control application did not ensure separation on its own.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial bank input smaller than the situation required, produced a slower divergence of the flight path than expected during the breakout. SP recognized that the separation rate was insufficient, increased the input in a timely manner and established positive separation with no IP intervention. The final geometry was correct, but the initial input needed reinforcement.
texts.3: SP applied timely and proper control inputs at breakout initiation, establishing an immediate and positive divergence of the aircraft flight path from the formation. The magnitude of the inputs matched the situation, and separation of the flight paths was assured from the first moment of the maneuver.
texts.4: SP applied a single decisive and correctly sized control input that produced unambiguous separation of the flight path with no follow-up adjustment required. The maneuver was smooth, free of any overshoot in bank or pitch, and the separation achieved was immediately evident to the formation.
texts.marginal: SP applied control inputs that were adequate to ensure separation, but the initial displacement was consistently at the lower end of what the situation required and had to be reinforced shortly afterwards. The pattern suggests a reluctance to commit fully to the first input. SP is expected to size the initial input to the situation so that separation is positive from the outset.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a tentative and progressively applied bank input, achieved separation only after the input was increased to an effective value, at the edge of what timely separation allows. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size the initial input to the situation so separation is positive from the outset.
texts_at.2: SP, due to an initial bank input smaller than the situation required, produced a slower divergence of the flight path than expected before recognizing the shortfall and increasing the input in a timely manner. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the initial input to the situation so separation is positive from the outset.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief hesitation before the input reached its full size, applied timely and proper control inputs at breakout initiation, establishing an immediate and positive divergence of the aircraft flight path. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the initial input to the situation so separation is positive from the outset.

texts_above.2: SP produced a slower divergence of the flight path than expected at first before recognizing the shortfall and increasing the input in a timely manner, establishing positive separation with no IP intervention. Sizing the first input to the situation, rather than reinforcing it afterward, would make that increase unnecessary. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable initial-input sizing for separation.
texts_above.3: SP applied timely and proper control inputs at breakout initiation, establishing an immediate and positive divergence of the aircraft flight path with the magnitude matched to the situation. The initial input already matches the situation closely; only the smallest reinforcement is still needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good initial-input sizing for separation.
texts_above.4: SP applied a single decisive and correctly sized control input that produced unambiguous separation of the flight path with no follow-up adjustment required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior initial-input sizing for separation.

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of communication of the recognized problem to the rest of the formation, did not inform the formation leader that a breakout was being flown. The leader continued to manoeuvre on the assumption that the wingman remained in position, and the IP had to make the call to restore a common picture of the flight. The requirement to inform the formation leader in time was not met at any point of the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to an indirect and delayed transmission instead of a direct statement of the action being taken, did not inform the formation leader in time. The call was made only after the IP prompted for it, and by then the breakout was already well developed. The formation leader was left without the information at the moment it was required.
texts.2: SP, due to prioritizing the control inputs and delaying the radio until after the turn was established, informed the formation leader later than required. SP recognized the omission without any prompting and passed a clear and correct call while the separation was still developing. The information reached the leader in usable time, but not at the first opportunity.
texts.3: SP informed the formation leader in time, passing a clear and standard call as the breakout was initiated. The transmission stated the action being taken so that the leader could account for the wingman without any further query.
texts.4: SP passed the breakout call immediately at initiation, in concise standard phraseology, so that the formation leader had complete awareness of the wingman action from the first second. Radio work was integrated with the flying without any detriment to either.
texts.marginal: SP informed the formation leader within acceptable time on every breakout, but the call consistently followed the control input by a noticeable margin rather than accompanying it. Phraseology is correct but delivered only once the aircraft is settled. SP is expected to pass the call as the maneuver is initiated, since its value to the leader decreases with every second of delay.

texts_at.1: SP, due to an indirect and delayed transmission instead of a direct statement of the action being taken, informed the formation leader at the edge of usable time, with the breakout already well developed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pass the call as the maneuver is initiated, since its value to the leader decreases with every second of delay.
texts_at.2: SP, due to prioritizing the control inputs and delaying the radio until after the turn was established, informed the formation leader later than required before recognizing the omission unprompted and passing a clear, correct call while separation was still developing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pass the call as the maneuver is initiated, since its value to the leader decreases with every second of delay.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief pause before keying the transmission, informed the formation leader in time, passing a clear and standard call as the breakout was initiated. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to pass the call as the maneuver is initiated, since its value to the leader decreases with every second of delay.

texts_above.2: SP informed the formation leader a little later than required before recognizing the omission unprompted and passing a clear, correct call while separation was still developing. Passing the call as the control input is made, rather than after the turn settles, would close that gap. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured breakout-call timing to the leader.
texts_above.3: SP informed the formation leader in time, passing a clear and standard call as the breakout was initiated that stated the action being taken. The call already accompanies the maneuver closely; only the smallest margin of delay remains. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise breakout-call timing to the leader.
texts_above.4: SP passed the breakout call immediately at initiation, in concise standard phraseology, giving the formation leader complete awareness of the wingman action from the first second. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate breakout-call timing to the leader.

error_modes.label: Visual contact and position awareness relative to the 3/9 line

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft position relative to the formation leader, did not identify that visual contact had been lost and that a breakout was therefore imposed. The aircraft was allowed to progress in front of the 3/9 line with no separating action taken and with the position of the leader unknown to SP. The IP intervened to establish separation and to re-acquire the visual picture.
texts.1: SP, due to a degraded picture of the relative position after the closure developed, did not recognize the imminent loss of visual contact as a condition requiring the breakout. The maneuver was flown only after the IP identified the geometry and directed it, with the aircraft already at the 3/9 line. Recognition of the situation depended entirely on IP input rather than on SP assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan momentarily directed inside the cockpit, was slow to appreciate the developing closure and the degradation of the visual picture on the formation leader. SP re-acquired the picture, recognized that the condition for a breakout was being met and executed the separation without IP intervention. Awareness was recovered in time, though the geometry had already begun to develop.
texts.3: SP maintained continuous awareness of the aircraft position relative to the formation leader and of the quality of the visual contact throughout. The condition requiring a breakout was assessed correctly against the 3/9 line and the state of visual contact, and the maneuver was flown on the basis of that assessment.
texts.4: SP held an exact picture of the relative geometry at all times, tracking closure and the 3/9 line without any degradation of the visual contact. The assessment of whether a breakout was imposed was made accurately and well ahead of the situation, and the separation was flown on SP judgment alone.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the required awareness of the relative position and of the visual contact, but the assessment of the closure was consistently made late in the geometry, with the picture being rebuilt rather than continuously held. Attention is returning to the leader in discrete checks rather than being sustained. SP is expected to keep a continuous picture so that the condition for a breakout is recognized before the geometry develops.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a degraded picture of the relative position after the closure developed, recognized the imminent loss of visual contact at the edge of what the standard allows, with the geometry already close to the 3/9 line. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep a continuous picture so the condition for a breakout is recognized before the geometry develops.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a scan momentarily directed inside the cockpit, was slow to appreciate the developing closure before re-acquiring the picture and executing the separation without IP intervention. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep a continuous picture so the condition for a breakout is recognized before the geometry develops.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in updating the picture as the closure developed, maintained continuous awareness of the aircraft position relative to the formation leader, assessing the condition requiring a breakout correctly against the 3/9 line. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep a continuous picture so the condition for a breakout is recognized before the geometry develops.

texts_above.2: SP was a little slow to appreciate the developing closure before re-acquiring the picture, recognizing that the condition for a breakout was being met and executing the separation without IP intervention. Keeping the scan on the relative position through the closure, rather than returning to it, would remove that lag. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent relative-position awareness ahead of the 3/9 line.
texts_above.3: SP maintained continuous awareness of the aircraft position relative to the formation leader and of the quality of visual contact, assessing the condition requiring a breakout correctly against the 3/9 line. The awareness is already continuous through the geometry; only the smallest gap in the scan remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined relative-position awareness ahead of the 3/9 line.
texts_above.4: SP held an exact picture of the relative geometry at all times, tracking closure and the 3/9 line without any degradation of visual contact and flying the separation on the SP's own judgment alone. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless relative-position awareness ahead of the 3/9 line.

error_modes.label: Stabilization and aircraft control after separation

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs continued past the point at which separation had been achieved, did not stabilize the aircraft after the breakout. Bank, pitch and airspeed were left uncontrolled simultaneously, with more than one parameter beyond its limit and no correction being applied. The IP intervened on the controls to establish steady flight clear of the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to attention remaining on the position of the formation after the separation was assured, did not re-establish controlled flight promptly following the breakout. Parameters remained at their limits and were brought back only after the IP called each one in turn. Stabilization was achieved late and only through verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed resumption of the instrument cross-check after clearing the formation, allowed the aircraft parameters to sit outside the tight band once the breakout was complete. The deviations remained between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP re-established the cross-check on his own initiative and returned the aircraft to steady flight without IP input.
texts.3: SP stabilized the aircraft immediately once separation had been achieved, resuming the instrument cross-check and holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight band. The transition from the separating maneuver to steady flight clear of the formation was controlled and deliberate.
texts.4: SP transitioned from the breakout to fully stabilized flight with no perceptible gap, all parameters settling on their values at once and remaining there. The aircraft was left in an ideal state from which further instructions from the formation leader or the IP could be accepted immediately.
texts.marginal: SP stabilized the aircraft within standards after the breakout, but the parameters were allowed to wander for several seconds before the cross-check was resumed and the deviations were near the outer part of the band during that period. The maneuver is being treated as finished at the point of separation rather than at the point of stabilization. SP is expected to close out the breakout by re-establishing the cross-check without that pause.

texts_at.1: SP, due to attention remaining on the position of the formation after separation was assured, brought the parameters back to their limits only after each was called in turn, with the aircraft at the edge of the tight band. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to close out the breakout by re-establishing the cross-check without that pause.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a delayed resumption of the instrument cross-check after clearing the formation, let the aircraft parameters sit between the code 3 and code 1 limits before re-establishing the cross-check on the SP's own initiative. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to close out the breakout by re-establishing the cross-check without that pause.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief pause before the instrument cross-check resumed, stabilized the aircraft immediately once separation had been achieved, resuming the instrument cross-check and holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight band. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to close out the breakout by re-establishing the cross-check without that pause.

texts_above.2: SP let the aircraft parameters sit between the code 3 and code 1 limits briefly before re-establishing the cross-check on the SP's own initiative and returning the aircraft to steady flight, without IP input. Resuming the cross-check the instant the formation is clear, rather than after a pause, would tighten that recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to good post-separation stabilization technique.
texts_above.3: SP stabilized the aircraft immediately once separation had been achieved, resuming the instrument cross-check and holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight band. The transition to steady flight is already controlled and deliberate; only the smallest pause before the cross-check resumes is left. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good post-separation stabilization technique.
texts_above.4: SP transitioned from the breakout to fully stabilized flight with no perceptible gap, all parameters settling on their values at once and remaining there. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent post-separation stabilization technique.

error_modes.label: Clearing in the direction of the break and manoeuvring away from Number 1 last known position

texts.0: SP, due to a break initiated without clearing in the direction of the break, manoeuvred toward the last known position of Number 1 instead of away from it. The direction selected did not ensure immediate separation and the flight path was driven back across the formation, with the exit heading finishing more than 10 degrees on the wrong side of the direction required. The IP took the controls and reversed the direction of the manoeuvre to open the geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to a clearing action taken only after bank had already been established, began the break in a direction that did not clearly move the aircraft away from the last known position of Number 1. The direction was corrected only after the IP verbally directed the break the other way, and the exit heading settled about 10 degrees off the required separation vector. Separation was eventually obtained, but the choice of direction was not SP work.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried clearing glance in the direction of the break, initially selected a break vector that only partially moved the aircraft away from the last known position of Number 1. SP recognized that the divergence was weak, cleared again and adjusted the break, finishing about 7 degrees off the ideal separation heading with no IP intervention. The correction was timely and the geometry never became convergent.
texts.3: SP cleared in the direction of the break before applying bank and manoeuvred positively away from the last known position of Number 1. The direction chosen ensured immediate separation and the exit heading was held within 5 degrees of the vector required to open the geometry.
texts.4: SP cleared the airspace in the direction of the break as part of the initiating action and selected without hesitation the vector that moved the aircraft directly away from the last known position of Number 1. error_modes.label: Use of power and speed brake to maintain safe manoeuvring airspeed and expedite separation

texts.0: SP, due to a breakout flown on stick alone with no throttle or speed brake movement, did not use power as required to maintain safe manoeuvring airspeed while expediting the separation. Bank and back stick were held while the airspeed decayed more than 20 knots below the formation airspeed and the rate of separation stagnated. The IP intervened on the throttle to restore energy and complete the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a late recognition that the manoeuvre was consuming energy, did not advance power in time to hold safe manoeuvring airspeed during the break. Power was added only after the IP called the decaying airspeed, by which point the excursion had reached about 20 knots and the separation had been slower than the situation demanded. Energy management during the break depended on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power advance made after the bank rather than with it, allowed the airspeed to fall about 15 knots below the formation airspeed while separation was being generated. SP recognized the decay on the airspeed indicator, added power and cleaned the manoeuvre up without IP intervention. Safe manoeuvring airspeed was restored before the deviation grew further.
texts.3: SP used power and, where appropriate, speed brake as required during the break, holding the airspeed within 10 knots of the value needed for safe manoeuvring while expediting the separation. Energy was managed as part of the manoeuvre rather than as an afterthought, and the rate of separation was never limited by a lack of airspeed.
texts.4: SP moved the throttle with the first control input of the break, so that safe manoeuvring airspeed was preserved throughout and the separation was expedited without any airspeed excursion of note. The use of power and speed brake was matched exactly to the separation required, with negligible variation from the target airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP maintained safe manoeuvring airspeed during the break within standards, but the throttle was consistently moved after the manoeuvre had begun and the airspeed was allowed to sag toward the lower edge of the acceptable band before power was added. The trend is toward treating energy as a recovery item rather than part of the break. SP is expected to lead the manoeuvre with power so that the separation is expedited from the outset.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a late recognition that the manoeuvre was consuming energy, let the airspeed excursion reach about 20 knots before power was added to hold safe manoeuvring airspeed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lead the manoeuvre with power so the separation is expedited from the outset.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a power advance made after the bank rather than with it, let the airspeed fall about 15 knots below the formation airspeed before recognizing the decay and adding power without IP intervention. error_modes.label: Abrupt oversized break inputs and the assumption that a breakout requires a high-G turn

texts.0: SP, due to the assumption that a breakout always requires an abrupt high-G turn away from Number 1, applied a rapid increase in back stick pressure together with abrupt rudder and an abrupt advance to MAX power. The aircraft rolled past the desired bank angle and the nose was pulled well through, producing an altitude departure of more than 300 feet from the formation altitude and an airspeed excursion beyond 20 knots. The IP intervened on the controls to unload the aircraft and re-establish a controlled separation.
texts.1: SP, due to an abrupt application of rudder and a rapid increase in back stick pressure at break initiation, rolled past the desired bank angle and aggravated the manoeuvre rather than simply separating. The inputs were reduced to a controlled level only after the IP verbally directed a smoother break, with the altitude excursion reaching about 300 feet and the airspeed about 20 knots off. The separation was achieved, but through an abrupt manoeuvre that was not what the situation required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial overreaction at break initiation, applied more back stick and bank than the geometry called for and momentarily exceeded the intended bank angle. SP recognized the overcontrol, relaxed the back pressure and settled the manoeuvre, containing the altitude excursion to about 200 feet with no IP intervention. The separation was positive and the manoeuvre finished under control.
texts.3: SP flew the breakout with control inputs sized to the situation, avoiding any rapid increase in back stick pressure or abrupt rudder application and matching the bank angle to the separation actually required. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the formation altitude and airspeed within 10 knots throughout the manoeuvre.
texts.4: SP recognized that the situation did not call for an abrupt high-G turn and separated with a smooth, correctly sized manoeuvre, free of rudder abruptness and of any advance of power beyond what was needed. The aircraft was flown precisely to the intended bank angle with negligible altitude or airspeed excursion while separation was positively established.
texts.marginal: SP kept the break inputs within standards, but the manoeuvre was consistently flown more aggressively than the geometry required, with back stick pressure applied quickly and bank angle taken slightly past the intended value before being settled. The pattern suggests a default toward the abrupt high-G interpretation of a breakout. SP is expected to size the manoeuvre to the separation actually needed rather than reaching for the most aggressive option.

texts_at.1: SP, due to an abrupt application of rudder and a rapid increase in back stick pressure at break initiation, rolled past the desired bank angle with the altitude excursion reaching about 300 feet and the airspeed about 20 knots off before the inputs were reduced to a controlled level. error_modes.label: Anticipation of disorientation when passing under Number 1 or viewing through the top of the canopy

texts.0: SP, due to no anticipation of the disorientation associated with passing under Number 1 and viewing the leader through the top of the canopy, fixated on the leader with the head fully back and lost the attitude picture. Sight of Number 1 was lost during the break, the aircraft was allowed to depart more than 300 feet from the formation altitude and the exit heading wandered beyond 10 degrees with no instrument cross-check taken. The IP intervened to recover the attitude and re-establish the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a failure to anticipate the disorientation while passing beneath Number 1, held the visual on the leader through the top of the canopy without any reference to the attitude indicator. The developing altitude excursion of about 300 feet and the heading wander were arrested only after the IP called for an instrument cross-check. SP kept the leader in sight, but attitude control during that phase relied on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary disorientation as the leader moved to the top of the canopy during the break, allowed the pitch and bank picture to degrade and the altitude to depart about 200 feet. SP recognized the sensation, cross-checked the attitude indicator and re-established the flight path in a timely manner with no IP intervention. Both the visual and the aircraft control were recovered before the deviation grew.
texts.3: SP anticipated the disorientation associated with passing under Number 1 and used caution while the leader was viewed through the top of the canopy, backing the visual picture with attitude reference. Altitude was contained within 150 feet and heading within 5 degrees of the intended values while sight of the leader was maintained throughout.
texts.4: SP briefed and expected the disorientation of the underneath pass, alternating between the visual on Number 1 and the attitude reference so that neither the sight of the leader nor the flight path was compromised at any point. Deviations in altitude and heading during that phase of the break were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained aircraft control while passing under Number 1 within standards, but the head was held back on the leader for long periods with the attitude cross-check delayed until a deviation had begun to build. The trend is toward absorbing the disorientation rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to plan the underneath pass in advance and interleave the attitude reference with the visual on the leader.

error_modes.label: Blind call content and action taken when the blind call is not acknowledged

texts.0: SP, due to a transmission that gave neither call sign nor current altitude, made a lost sight call that did not allow Number 1 to deconflict the flight paths. With no acknowledgement received, SP continued to hold heading and altitude instead of manoeuvring away from the last known position of Number 1 and altering altitude, leaving the aircraft more than 300 feet from the formation altitude and inside the leader turn. The IP transmitted the correct blind call and directed the altitude change.
texts.1: SP, due to a blind call transmitted without the current altitude, gave Number 1 an incomplete picture of the vertical geometry after sight was lost. The altitude was added and the aircraft manoeuvred away from the last known position only after the IP directed it, with the vertical separation still at about 300 feet when the action was finally taken. The procedure was completed, but the content of the call and the follow-up action came from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial call made with the call sign and the word blind but with the altitude appended late, delayed the moment at which Number 1 could build the vertical picture. SP recognized the omission, immediately restated the call with current altitude and, on receiving no prompt acknowledgement, manoeuvred away from the last known position and altered altitude without IP intervention. The correction was made in time and separation was assured.
texts.3: SP transmitted a complete blind call with call sign and current altitude as soon as sight was lost, and on the absence of a timely acknowledgement manoeuvred away from the last known position of Number 1 while altering altitude. The vertical separation established was positive and the exchange with the leader followed the prescribed content.
texts.4: SP made an immediate and correctly formatted blind call with call sign, blind and current altitude, adding the turn direction and heading where it helped the leader build the picture. Without waiting on the acknowledgement, SP altered altitude and manoeuvred clear of the last known position, so that flight path deconfliction was assured independently of the radio.
texts.marginal: SP made the blind call with the required content and altered altitude within standards, but the altitude element was consistently the last item of the transmission and the manoeuvre away from the last known position waited on the acknowledgement rather than starting with the call. The trend is toward treating the radio as the primary means of deconfliction. SP is expected to state the altitude within the initial call and to begin the separating manoeuvre without waiting on a reply.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a blind call transmitted without the current altitude, left the vertical separation at about 300 feet before the altitude was added and the manoeuvre away from the last known position was flown. The content of the call is already complete on first transmission; only the smallest delay in the follow-up manoeuvre remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise blind-call content discipline.

error_modes.label: Excessive range during the breakout and the directed roll out and visual sequence

texts.0: SP, due to a break continued far beyond the point at which safe separation had been assured, obtained excessive range on Number 1 and lost the visual on the leader altogether. The roll out directed by Number 1 was not acknowledged and not flown, and the exit heading finished more than 10 degrees beyond the value that would have preserved the picture. The IP took the controls, rolled out and re-acquired the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to holding bank after the separation requirement had already been satisfied, allowed the range on Number 1 to open excessively during the practice breakout. The roll out was flown and the visual call made only after the IP repeated the direction from Number 1, with the exit heading about 10 degrees past the intended value. The recovery of the picture depended on IP prompting rather than on SP judgement.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly prolonged break, opened more range on Number 1 than the exercise required before the situation was reassessed. SP recognized the trend, rolled out on the direction from Number 1, acknowledged it and called visual, finishing about 7 degrees off the intended exit heading with no IP intervention. The formation picture was recovered in good time and further direction was awaited.
texts.3: SP flew the breakout to the point at which safe separation was established and then held the geometry without opening excessive range on Number 1. The roll out directed by the leader was acknowledged and flown, the visual call was made and the exit heading was contained within 5 degrees of the intended value while further direction was awaited.
texts.4: SP stopped the break exactly where safe separation was assured, keeping Number 1 comfortably in sight and the range appropriate for the exercise throughout. The roll out was acknowledged and flown immediately, the visual call followed at once, and deviations from the intended exit heading were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the range on Number 1 within acceptable limits, but the break was consistently held a little past the point at which separation had already been achieved, so the picture on the leader was thinning by the time the roll out came. SP is expected to reassess the geometry continuously and stop the break as soon as safe separation exists.

texts_above.3: SP flew the breakout to the point at which safe separation was established and then held the geometry without opening excessive range, containing the exit heading within about 3 degrees of the intended value. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined range-versus-separation judgment on the practice breakout.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless range-versus-separation judgment on the practice breakout.

texts.0: SP, due to treating a small and controllable 3/9 line overshoot as a mandatory breakout condition, abandoned a recoverable rejoin although the flight paths were not convergent and visual contact on Number 1 was never in doubt. The unnecessary manoeuvre took the aircraft more than 300 feet off the formation altitude and more than 10 degrees off the rejoin geometry, and the exercise had to be reset. The IP intervened to stop the manoeuvre and restore the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect assessment of a minor 3/9 line overshoot, initiated a breakout that the geometry did not require, with nose-tail separation intact and the leader in sight throughout. The manoeuvre was stopped only after the IP identified that the flight paths were not convergent, by which time the departure from the formation altitude had reached about 300 feet. texts.2: SP, due to an initial overreaction to a controllable overshoot across the 3/9 line, began to displace away from the formation before completing the assessment of the flight paths. texts.3: SP distinguished a small controllable 3/9 line overshoot from a condition requiring a breakout, confirming that the flight paths were not convergent and that visual contact and nose-tail separation were maintained. texts.4: SP assessed the overshoot accurately as it developed, judged that the flight paths were divergent and that visual contact and nose-tail separation were assured, and managed the geometry inside the rejoin without any unnecessary departure from the formation. Deviations in altitude and rejoin line during the recovery were negligible.

error_modes.label: Responsibility for separation until acknowledgement and prohibition on rejoining until directed

texts.0: SP, due to treating the separation as complete the moment the aircraft was clear, began to close back on the formation without any acknowledgement of the breakout, without confirmation of visual contact by Number 1 and without altitude separation established. SP rejoined without being directed by Number 1, bringing the aircraft back inside 300 feet of the formation altitude while the leader was still manoeuvring predictably on the assumption of separation. The IP intervened to stop the closure and restore the spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to an early assumption that the breakout had been acknowledged, started to reduce the separation before Number 1 had confirmed visual contact or established altitude separation. The closure was stopped and the correct spacing re-established only after the IP directed it, with the vertical separation already reduced to about 300 feet. The discipline of holding position until directed was not maintained by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to an over-eagerness to get the formation back together, began to shape toward a rejoin line before the direction from Number 1 had been received. SP recognized that no rejoin had been directed, arrested the closure and held safe separation with about 200 feet of vertical spacing preserved and no IP intervention. The rejoin was subsequently flown only on the direction of the leader.
texts.3: SP maintained safe separation after the breakout until Number 1 acknowledged the manoeuvre, confirmed visual contact or established altitude separation, and made no attempt to rejoin until directed by the leader. The spacing held during that period remained comfortably outside 150 feet vertically and the rejoin was initiated only on direction.
texts.4: SP held the separation established by the breakout without any drift back toward the formation, waiting for the acknowledgement, the visual confirmation or the altitude separation from Number 1 before considering any change. The rejoin was flown only after it was directed, and the spacing maintained throughout the interval varied negligibly.
texts.marginal: SP held safe separation until directed and did not rejoin on its own initiative, but the spacing was allowed to erode slowly during the wait and the aircraft was consistently shaped toward the rejoin line before any direction had been given. The pattern points toward anticipating the rejoin rather than holding the separation. SP is expected to preserve the spacing unchanged until Number 1 acknowledges, confirms visual or directs the rejoin.

texts_at.1: SP, due to an early assumption that the breakout had been acknowledged, reduced the separation with the vertical spacing already down to about 300 feet before the closure was stopped. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to preserve the spacing unchanged until Number 1 acknowledges, confirms visual or directs the rejoin.
texts_at.2: SP, due to an over-eagerness to get the formation back together, began to shape toward a rejoin line before the direction from Number 1 had been received, before recognizing that no rejoin had been directed and arresting the closure with about 200 feet of vertical spacing preserved. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to preserve the spacing unchanged until Number 1 acknowledges, confirms visual or directs the rejoin.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief eagerness to shape toward the rejoin line ahead of the direction, maintained safe separation after the breakout until Number 1 acknowledged the manoeuvre, confirmed visual contact or established altitude separation, holding spacing outside about 100 feet vertically. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to preserve the spacing unchanged until Number 1 acknowledges, confirms visual or directs the rejoin.

texts_above.2: SP began to shape toward a rejoin line briefly before the direction from Number 1 had been received, then recognized that no rejoin had been directed, arresting the closure with about 200 feet of vertical spacing preserved and no IP intervention. Holding the spacing unchanged until the direction is received, rather than shaping toward it, would remove that early move. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound hold-until-directed discipline after the breakout.
texts_above.3: SP maintained safe separation after the breakout until Number 1 acknowledged the manoeuvre, confirmed visual contact or established altitude separation, holding spacing outside about 100 feet vertically and rejoining only on direction. The discipline of holding position already extends through the wait; only the smallest early shaping remains to be removed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed hold-until-directed discipline after the breakout.
texts_above.4: SP held the separation established by the breakout without any drift back toward the formation, waiting for acknowledgement, visual confirmation or direction with the spacing varying negligibly throughout the interval. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional hold-until-directed discipline after the breakout.
